lesson.title: Nothing Is Created, Nothing Is Destroyed
lesson.summary: Explains why the total mass and total energy of a chemical system stay constant during a reaction, and shows how this bookkeeping rule underlies balancing equations and predicting heat changes.
lesson.body:
You already know that energy can move between objects as heat or as work, changing form without disappearing. Conservation laws take that idea one step further: they say that for a system that isn't exchanging matter or energy with its surroundings, certain totals never change no matter what happens inside. In chemistry, the two totals that matter most are the total mass of all the substances present and the total energy of the system. Reactions can look dramatic ,  flames, fizzing, color changes ,  but underneath, the amount of "stuff" and the amount of energy are simply being reorganized, not gained or lost.

Start with mass. A chemical reaction is really just atoms breaking old bonds and forming new ones; the atoms themselves don't vanish or appear from nowhere. Since mass ultimately comes from the number and identity of atoms present, and that number doesn't change, the total mass before the reaction must equal the total mass after it. Take methane burning in oxygen: CH₄ + 2 O₂ → CO₂ + 2 H₂O. On the reactant side, one mole of CH₄ (16 g) plus two moles of O₂ (2 × 32 g = 64 g) gives 80 g. On the product side, one mole of CO₂ (44 g) plus two moles of H₂O (2 × 18 g = 36 g) also gives 80 g. Every carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen atom that started as methane and oxygen ends up somewhere in the carbon dioxide and water ,  none are lost, so the masses match exactly. This is precisely why you can balance chemical equations by adjusting coefficients rather than subscripts: you're not allowed to destroy or invent atoms, only rearrange how many of each molecule are involved.

Energy conservation works the same way but tracks a different quantity. The first law of thermodynamics says the total energy of an isolated system stays constant, even as energy shifts between forms ,  chemical potential energy stored in bonds, kinetic energy of moving particles, and energy exchanged as heat or work. When methane burns, the bonds in the products (CO₂ and H₂O) are more stable, lower in potential energy, than the bonds in the reactants. That difference in stored energy doesn't disappear; it converts into kinetic energy of the surrounding particles, which you detect as heat and a rise in temperature. Nothing new energy was manufactured by the flame ,  potential energy simply became thermal energy. In an endothermic process, the reverse happens: energy absorbed from the surroundings as heat gets stored as chemical potential energy in newly formed, less stable bonds.

Together, these two conservation laws give chemistry its predictive power. Because mass is conserved, you can use a balanced equation to calculate exactly how many grams of product will form from a given amount of reactant. Because energy is conserved, you can measure the heat released or absorbed in a reaction and know that quantity reflects a real change in chemical potential energy, not an approximation. Every calorimetry calculation and every stoichiometric mass calculation you'll do later rests on trusting that these totals genuinely hold ,  that whatever mass or energy you start with is still there, just relocated, when the reaction is finished.
